claim: GapR preferentially recognizes overtwisted DNA in vitro as demonstrated by topological assays where increasing amounts of GapR led to formation of positively supercoiled plasmid.
source: Increasing amounts of GapR led to a gradual, but marked change in plasmid topology (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to the formation of positively supercoiled plasmid as determined using two-dimensional chloroquine electrophoresis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from topological assays and two-dimensional chloroquine electrophoresis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GapR constrains positive superhelical density and prevents writhing, as shown by increased DNA extension in magnetic tweezer experiments at positive σ.
source: After introducing positive σ, we observed significantly increased extension of GapR-bound DNA compared to naked DNA (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F). These results indicate that GapR constrains the added positive σ, preventing writhing, and increasing DNA extension (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by magnetic tweezer experimental data showing DNA extension measurements at various superhelical densities, presented in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: GapR-DNA complexes at negative superhelical density are less stable than those at positive superhelical density, as evidenced by larger dynamical fluctuations in DNA length.
source: Moreover, in individual experiments, the length of GapR-bound DNA molecules dynamically fluctuated at negative σ as a function of time, leading to a larger standard deviation of extension at negative σ than for positive σ (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), and with a substantially larger coefficient of variation in DNA length at negative σ compared to positive σ or naked DNA (Figure 1F). Therefore, the structures of GapR-DNA complexes at negative σ are less stable than those at positive σ.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course measurements and statistical analysis of DNA length variations shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1F.

claim: Ectopic expression of GapR-3xFLAG in E. coli did not affect growth rate, alter global transcription, or change expression of known supercoiling-sensitive genes.
source: Importantly, GapR induction did not affect the growth rate of E. coli, alter global transcription, or the expression of known supercoiling-sensitive genes (Peter et al., 2004; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on growth rates, transcriptional profiles, and expression of supercoiling-sensitive genes, with citation to Peter et al., 2004, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: In E. coli, GapR binds at the 3' ends of highly expressed transcription units in a transcription-dependent manner.
source: At a highly expressed ribosomal protein operon (Figure 2B), we observed GapR binding from just inside the 3' end of rplQ to ~2 kb downstream (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1G). To test if this GapR binding was transcription-dependent, we treated cells with the RNA polymerase inhibitor rifampicin for 20 min before performing GapR ChIP. Consistent with our results in Caulobacter (Guo et al., 2018), rifampicin largely abrogated GapR binding downstream of rplQ (Figure 2B, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data before and after rifampicin treatment shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, with citation to previous work (Guo et al., 2018).

claim: GapR binding at the 3' ends of transcription units in E. coli correlates with transcriptional strength.
source: In contrast, at 3' ends, GapR binding was dependent on expression, with highly expressed TUs having significantly increased GapR occupancy relative to within the TU (t-test, p<10−13 for all expression cutoffs, Figure 2D, E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of GapR ChIP data at different expression levels shown in Figure 2D, E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Dimeric GapR1-76 binds DNA but does not recognize DNA topology, as shown by topological assays.
source: Whereas full-length GapR trapped positive supercoils, GapR1-76 did not alter plasmid topology (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, see also Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B). We conclude that dimeric GapR1-76 binds DNA but no longer recognizes DNA topology, indicating that positive supercoiling recognition requires a tetrameric conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by topological assay data comparing full-length GapR and GapR1-76 shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GapR1-76 ChIP profiles do not correlate with full-length GapR ChIP profiles in E. coli, demonstrating that full-length GapR is not simply binding accessible DNA.
source: Notably, GapR1-76 does not bind at the 3' ends of TUs as seen with full-length GapR (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). In fact, the ChIP profiles of GapR1-76 and full-length GapR were not correlated (Figure 3C), demonstrating that full-length GapR is not simply bound to accessible DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing GapR and GapR1-76 shown in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In E. coli, GapR is enriched at convergently oriented transcription units compared to divergently oriented or intragenic regions.
source: Convergently oriented regions had higher GapR signal compared to intragenic or divergently oriented regions (t-test, p<10−9, Figure 3F, examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G), whereas GapR1-76 bound similarly in convergently and divergently oriented regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of GapR ChIP data at regions with different transcriptional orientations shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figures.

claim: GapR enrichment between convergently oriented transcription units in E. coli is transcription-dependent.
source: Importantly, GapR enrichment between convergently oriented TUs was dependent on transcription (t-test, p<10−27; Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of transcription-dependent changes in GapR ChIP shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Regions with the highest transcription-dependent changes in GapR in E. coli are highly enriched for convergently oriented transcription units.
source: Regions with the highest transcription-dependent changes in GapR were highly enriched for convergently oriented TUs compared to regions with the lowest transcription-dependence or intergenic regions (Fisher's exact test, p<10−35 and p<10−14, respectively, Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) comparing transcriptional orientations at regions with different GapR enrichment levels shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Expression of GapR-3xFLAG in S. cerevisiae did not significantly alter the transcriptional profile or activate stress response pathways.
source: As in bacteria, (1) expression of GapR-3xFLAG did not significantly alter the transcriptional profile of yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), with less than twofold changes in genes that are supercoiling-sensitive (Pedersen et al., 2012) or involved in the general stress response (Pka1, Hog1, Hsf1, Yap1), the unfolded protein response, or the DNA damage response (Jaehnig et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, with citations to Pedersen et al., 2012 and Jaehnig et al., 2013.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR is enriched at the 3' ends of genes, with enrichment correlating with transcriptional strength.
source: Also as in bacteria, GapR was significantly enriched at the 3', but not the 5', ends of genes (Figure 4B). To determine if GapR is recognizing transcription-dependent positive supercoiling, we computationally compared our GapR-seq and RNA-seq profiles. We found that GapR enrichment at the 3' ends of genes was clearly correlated with transcriptional strength (t-test, p<10−25 for all expression cutoffs at 3' ends, Figure 4C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of GapR ChIP data at gene ends at different expression levels shown in Figure 4B, C, D.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR is enriched at regions of convergent transcription compared to divergent or intragenic regions.
source: Additionally, and again as found in E. coli, GapR was enriched at regions of convergent transcription compared to divergent or intragenic regions (Figure 4E, F, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data comparing different transcriptional orientations shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR occupancy between co-oriented genes correlates with transcription level of the upstream gene but not the downstream gene.
source: Indeed, we found that between co-oriented genes, GapR was correlated with the transcriptional level of the upstream gene but not the downstream gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K). Restricting this analysis to gene pairs in which the downstream gene is poorly expressed also showed that GapR occupancy only correlated with the transcription level of the upstream gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of GapR ChIP with upstream and downstream gene expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR binding changes in response to altered transcription during α-factor arrest, with increased enrichment at 3' ends of upregulated genes and decreased enrichment at 3' ends of downregulated genes.
source: As anticipated, GapR occupancy increased at the 3' ends of genes induced in α-factor and modestly decreased at the 3' ends of genes repressed by α-factor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). To better visualize these changes, we ordered genes by their change in expression in α-factor and plotted as a heatmap the change in GapR at each gene's 5' and 3' ends (Figure 5B). These heatmaps showed that upon α-factor treatment GapR binding was often substantially increased at the 3' ends of upregulated genes and decreased at the 3' ends of downregulated genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data comparing cells with and without α-factor treatment shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GapR can bind in heterochromatin regions in S. cerevisiae, such as the yeast mating cassettes.
source: We first examined GapR binding in heterochromatin, such as the yeast mating cassettes, and found that GapR can still access these relatively compacted loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at heterochromatic loci shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, positions of high GapR enrichment are found within 200 bp of nucleosomes.
source: We found that nucleosomes are often in close proximity to GapR peaks (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E), with positions of high GapR enrichment found within 200 bp of nucleosomes (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of GapR ChIP with MNase-seq data shown in Figure 5C, D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E, F.

claim: GapR enrichment in S. cerevisiae is not strongly correlated with DNase I hypersensitivity, indicating that DNA accessibility is not predictive of GapR enrichment.
source: Although there was some overlap between sites of GapR binding and DNase cleavage, there were many DNase-sensitive regions not bound by GapR, and many loci with high GapR ChIP that were not DNase-accessible (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E), indicating that DNA accessibility is not predictive of GapR enrichment.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of GapR ChIP with DNase-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: GapR-seq in S. cerevisiae shows little overlap or correlation with psoralen-based methods for detecting positive supercoiling.
source: We directly compared our GapR-seq to this prior data, but found little overlap or correlation between GapR-enriched sites and those regions de-enriched for psoralen intercalation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of GapR-seq data with published psoralen tiling array data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR accumulates at centromeres (CEN) upon α-factor arrest and when grown in glycerol.
source: In contrast, GapR accumulates at CEN upon α-factor arrest and when grown in glycerol, which extends G1 phase (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at centromeres under different growth conditions shown in Figure 6A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GapR occupancy at S. cerevisiae centromeres is highest immediately 5' of CEN and remains high ~500 bp to the 5' and 3' of CEN.
source: By aligning GapR enrichment over all 16 CEN, we found that GapR occupancy was highest immediately to the 5' of CEN, upstream of the first centromere determining element and remained high ~500 bp to the 5' and 3' of CEN, with a small 3' shoulder (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by aligned GapR ChIP data across all centromeres shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR is enriched at pericentromere boundaries marked by convergent genes.
source: In all media conditions, GapR was modestly to highly enriched between the convergent genes that mark pericentromere boundaries (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at pericentromere boundaries shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, cohesin-enriched regions are frequently associated with GapR binding.
source: Outside of pericentromeres, cohesin is also frequently, but not exclusively, associated with convergent genes. These cohesin-enriched regions were also bound by GapR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), supporting the idea that cohesin binding is associated with positive supercoiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of GapR ChIP with Scc1 ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In S. cerevisiae grown in glycerol, >90% of the top 500 cohesin peaks have significant neighboring GapR enrichment within 200 bp.
source: To systematically examine any relationship between positive supercoiling and cohesin, we generated heatmaps of GapR enrichment surrounding the 500 highest cohesin-bound regions, finding that >90% of all cohesin peaks in glycerol had significant neighboring GapR enrichment within 200 bp (GapR enrichment > µ + σ; Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis of GapR and Scc1 enrichment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR binds at two major peaks in the rDNA locus: one in the unique region at the 3' end and one within the rDNA ~1600 bp upstream of the ribosomal autonomously replicating sequence (rARS) coinciding with the replication fork barrier (RFB).
source: GapR binds at two major peaks in the rDNA locus: (1) one in the unique region at the 3' end of the rDNA locus, which likely arises from transcription of the last 35S rDNA repeat, and (2) one within the rDNA, ~1600 bp upstream of the ribosomal autonomously replicating sequence (rARS) that coincides with the replication fork barrier (RFB), with an additional minor peak over the rARS (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at the rDNA locus shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR is enriched within many autonomously replicating sequences (ARS) in cells treated with α-factor and grown in glycerol.
source: Because of the GapR enrichment near rARS, we asked whether GapR was enriched near other ARS and found that GapR was enriched within many ARS compared to intergenic sequences in cells treated with α-factor and grown in glycerol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at ARS shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR peaks are associated with Ty element terminal repeats (LTRs), with peaks of GapR centered just beyond each DRIP-seq peak marking R-loops.
source: To compare our GapR-seq to published S1-DRIP-seq data (Wahba et al., 2016), we aligned all 49 yeast Ty elements and examined R-loop formation and GapR binding. We observed two peaks of DNA-RNA hybrids centered on the LTRs of Ty elements, with the peaks of GapR centered just beyond each DRIP-seq peak (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of GapR ChIP with S1-DRIP-seq data (Wahba et al., 2016) shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GapR is highly enriched at telomeres containing Y' elements, with enrichment greatest over the telomeric repeats and remaining high ~500 bp towards centromeres, past the DNA-RNA hybrids.
source: Notably, GapR is also highly enriched at these telomeres, with enrichment greatest over the telomeric repeats and remaining high, ~500 bp towards centromeres, past the DNA-RNA hybrids (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR ChIP data at telomeres shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: The twin-domain model of supercoiling predicts that positive supercoils occur ahead of RNA polymerase and negative supercoils in its wake during transcription.
source: When the DNA duplex is unwound during transcription, positive supercoils occur ahead of the polymerase and negative supercoils in its wake, producing the 'twin-domain' model of supercoiling (Liu and Wang, 1987; Wu et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Wang, 1987 and Wu et al., 1988, which describe the twin-domain model.

claim: Topoisomerase activity is essential for DNA replication, with rapid removal of positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork necessary to prevent replisome arrest.
source: Topoisomerase activity is essential for DNA replication, with the rapid removal of the positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork necessary to prevent replisome arrest (Postow et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Postow et al., 2001.

claim: Psoralen-based methods preferentially crosslink to undertwisted, negatively supercoiled DNA.
source: More recently, supercoiling has been measured via preferential crosslinking of psoralen derivatives to undertwisted, negatively supercoiled DNA (Achar et al., 2020; Bermúdez et al., 2010; Kouzine et al., 2013; Lal et al., 2016; Naughton et al., 2013; Sinden et al., 1980; Teves and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing psoralen-based methods (Achar et al., 2020; Bermúdez et al., 2010; Kouzine et al., 2013; Lal et al., 2016; Naughton et al., 2013; Sinden et al., 1980; Teves and Henikoff, 2014).

claim: RNA polymerase, nucleosomes, DNA-binding proteins, or unwound DNA could each block psoralen intercalation and complicate interpretation of crosslinking efficiency.
source: However, RNA polymerase, nucleosomes, DNA-binding proteins, or unwound DNA could each block psoralen intercalation and complicate the interpretation of crosslinking efficiency (Bermúdez et al., 2010; Toussaint et al., 2005; Wellinger and Sogo, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bermúdez et al., 2010; Toussaint et al., 2005; and Wellinger and Sogo, 1998.

claim: Previous work in Caulobacter crescentus demonstrated that GapR localizes to the 3' ends of highly transcribed regions and is required, together with type II topoisomerases, to relax positively supercoiled DNA during replication.
source: Our previous work in the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus demonstrated that GapR localizes to the 3' ends of highly transcribed regions and is required, together with type II topoisomerases, to relax positively supercoiled DNA during replication (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Guo et al., 2018).

claim: A previous crystal structure of GapR captured it as a dimer-of-dimers that fully encircled DNA, without any base-specific contacts and with a narrow DNA-binding cavity that should preferentially accommodate overtwisted DNA.
source: In addition to these topological assays, our previous crystal structure (Guo et al., 2018) captured GapR as a dimer-of-dimers that fully encircled DNA, without any base-specific contacts and with a narrow DNA-binding cavity that should preferentially accommodate overtwisted DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous crystal structure (Guo et al., 2018) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Eukaryotic chromatin has been observed to have low torsional stiffness to positive torsional stress.
source: This provides an important check for applicability in eukaryotic chromatin, which has been observed to have low torsional stiffness to positive torsional stress (Le et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Le et al., 2019.

claim: Cohesin rapidly compacts positively supercoiled DNA in vitro.
source: Cohesin is a chromosome organizing protein complex that mediates sister chromatid cohesion, homologous recombination, and other diverse functions by topologically linking distant loci (Moronta-Gines et al., 2019). Cohesin accumulates between convergent genes, including those that define pericentromere boundaries, and rapidly compacts positively supercoiled DNA in vitro, suggesting that cohesin may preferentially associate with such DNA (Glynn et al., 2004; Lengronne et al., 2004; Paldi et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glynn et al., 2004; Lengronne et al., 2004; Paldi et al., 2020; and Sun et al., 2013.

claim: Positive supercoiling has been proposed to accumulate at yeast centromeres, with supercoiling constrained within the centromeric sequences (CEN) and stabilized by binding of the CBF3 complex and the centromeric histone H3 variant, CENP-A/Cse4.
source: In yeast, positive supercoiling has been proposed to accumulate at centromeres, with supercoiling constrained within the centromeric sequences (CEN) and stabilized by binding of the CBF3 complex and the centromeric histone H3 variant, CENP-A/Cse4 (Díaz-Ingelmo et al., 2015; Steiner and Henikoff, 2015; Verdaasdonk and Bloom, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Díaz-Ingelmo et al., 2015; Steiner and Henikoff, 2015; and Verdaasdonk and Bloom, 2011.

claim: Transcription of telomeric sequences produces a long, noncoding telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) that invades telomere DNA and mediates telomere maintenance.
source: DNA-RNA hybrids also occur at telomeres, where transcription of telomeric sequences produces a long, noncoding telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) that invades telomere DNA and mediates telomere maintenance (Balk et al., 2013; Graf et al., 2017; Luke and Lingner, 2009; Niehrs and Luke, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balk et al., 2013; Graf et al., 2017; Luke and Lingner, 2009; and Niehrs and Luke, 2020.

claim: GapR-seq provides a direct, high-resolution readout of positive supercoiling in living cells.
source: Altogether, our data strongly support the idea that GapR is recognizing overtwisted, positive supercoiled DNA in vivo. We propose that GapR-seq provides a direct, high-resolution readout of positive supercoiling in living cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Positive supercoils generated downstream of translocating RNA polymerase should be strongly associated with convergently oriented transcription units.
source: Because positive supercoils are generated downstream of translocating RNA polymerase, we hypothesized that these supercoils, and GapR, should be strongly associated with convergently oriented TUs (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the twin-domain model of supercoiling.

claim: R-loops may be extremely sensitive to supercoiling, as opening an R-loop in relaxed, topologically constrained DNA leads to formation of positive supercoiling elsewhere, which can impede R-loop formation.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that R-loops may be extremely sensitive to supercoiling as opening an R-loop in relaxed, topologically constrained DNA leads to the formation of positive supercoiling elsewhere, which can impede R-loop formation (Stolz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stolz et al., 2019.

claim: Positive supercoiling adjacent to TERRA hybrids could be a barrier to further melting of the DNA duplex and R-loop spreading.
source: We propose that positive supercoiling may be generated during R-loop formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H) and that positive supercoiling adjacent to TERRA hybrids could be a barrier to further melting of the DNA duplex and R-loop spreading (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the observed association between GapR and R-loops.

claim: Local overtwisted DNA could act as a barrier to prevent further expansion of R-loops.
source: Local overtwisted DNA could also act as a barrier to prevent further expansion of R-loops (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the observed association between GapR and R-loops.

claim: GapR-seq is applicable in any organism for investigating aspects of chromosome structure and organization not accessible by Hi-C or other existing methods.
source: Our results suggest that GapR-seq is a powerful approach, likely applicable in any organism, to investigate aspects of chromosome structure and organization not accessible by Hi-C or other existing methods.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the successful application of GapR-seq in both bacterial and eukaryotic organisms.

claim: Positive supercoiling is widespread in genomes, associated with transcription, and particularly enriched between convergently oriented genes.
source: Applying this method to Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we find that positive supercoiling is widespread, associated with transcription, and particularly enriched between convergently oriented genes, consistent with the 'twin-domain' model of supercoiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR-seq data from E. coli and S. cerevisiae presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In yeast, positive supercoils are associated with centromeres, cohesin-binding sites, autonomously replicating sites, and the borders of R-loops.
source: In yeast, we also find positive supercoils associated with centromeres, cohesin-binding sites, autonomously replicating sites, and the borders of R-loops (DNA-RNA hybrids).
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR-seq data from S. cerevisiae presented in the manuscript.

claim: Positive supercoiling is a pervasive feature of genomes, with remarkably similar patterns documented in bacteria and yeast.
source: This new method revealed that positive supercoiling is a pervasive feature of genomes, with remarkably similar patterns documented in bacteria and yeast.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of GapR-seq data from E. coli and S. cerevisiae.

claim: Positive supercoils accumulate in a transcription-dependent manner at the 3' ends of genes and are particularly enriched in regions where transcription is convergent.
source: Positive supercoils accumulate in a transcription-dependent manner at the 3' ends of genes and are particularly enriched in regions where transcription is convergent.
evidence: The claim is supported by GapR-seq data from both E. coli and S. cerevisiae.

claim: GapR may not be able to recognize regions more modestly twisted or more highly twisted, or if writhed structures form that are somehow constrained from interconverting to a twisted form.
source: GapR recognizes overtwisted DNA and, in our topological assays, binds to ~8.5° of twist (Guo et al., 2018). GapR may not be able to recognize regions more modestly twisted or more highly twisted, or if writhed structures form (e.g., plectonemic or solenoidal supercoils) that are somehow constrained from interconverting to a twisted form.
evidence: The claim is a caveat based on the known properties of GapR binding, with citation to Guo et al., 2018.

claim: AT-rich DNA can adopt intrinsically bent structures with narrowed minor grooves that may be recognized in a supercoiling-independent manner by GapR.
source: AT-rich DNA can adopt intrinsically bent structures with narrowed minor grooves that may be recognized in a supercoiling-independent manner by GapR (Arias‐Cartin et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2018; Haran and Mohanty, 2009; Huang et al., 2020; Ricci et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a caveat supported by citations to Arias‐Cartin et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2018; Haran and Mohanty, 2009; Huang et al., 2020; and Ricci et al., 2016.

claim: GapR-seq is working similarly in yeast chromatin as in bacterial chromosomes, despite the low stiffness to positive torsional stress observed in eukaryotic chromatin.
source: For the case of eukaryotic chromatin, one might be concerned about the effects on GapR-seq of the low stiffness to positive torsional stress observed in single-molecule studies (Le et al., 2019), but our observations of similar GapR-seq patterns in bacteria and in yeast suggest that GapR-seq is working similarly in yeast chromatin as in bacterial chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of GapR-seq patterns in bacteria and yeast, with citation to Le et al., 2019.

claim: GapR binding is insensitive to the large-scale conformation of DNA and instead senses DNA torque.
source: The likely reason for this is that because GapR binds to overtwisted DNA, GapR binding is insensitive to what the large-scale conformation of the DNA region is, be it plectonemic supercoils (as occurs in bacteria) or locally deformed nucleosome structures (thought to be the case in chromatin; Le et al., 2019), and is instead sensing the stress (DNA torque).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanism of GapR binding, with citation to Le et al., 2019.

claim: Regions of positive torsional stress in yeast chromatin likely have similar levels of DNA torque to those found in bacteria.
source: This in turn suggests that regions of positive torsional stress in yeast chromatin likely have similar levels of DNA torque to those found in bacteria, which is logical since the physical processes generating those torques are similar.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of GapR-seq patterns and the physical processes generating torque.
